name: lamplight
summary: Not a surface. The glow itself, painted as white streaks on black and drawn additively.
why: Every other material in this library answers 'what is this made of'. This one answers
'this is not made of anything' - it is the light coming off a lamp, which MU draws as a
quad hanging in front of the model with a soft white smear on it, added to whatever is
behind rather than covering it. The black is not a colour, it is the part that adds
nothing.
Emissive: it is lit by nothing and lights nothing. Its brightness is its own. A glow that
takes the sun into account goes dark at night, which is exactly backwards.
Metallic 0.0 and roughness 1.0, which are both meaningless here and are set to the values
that do the least: nothing should produce a highlight on a surface that has no surface.
No grain, and for a firmer reason than foliage's. Foliage has no normal because its shape
is its alpha; this has none because relief on a glow is a category error. Light does not
have bumps.
It does not light the scene either. That is the emitter's job, declared separately on the
object - see StreetLight01 - because a light and a picture of a light are two different
things and MU keeps them apart too: the glow submesh is drawn by the renderer and the
lamp is registered with the terrain.
Brighter than white, at 3.2, and that is what makes it read as light rather than as a
panel. The frame blooms what is over one - a lamp, a window, the sun off a blade, the
only things in a town brighter than white - and a glow sitting at exactly one never
crossed it. So the softness around a lit window was missing for a reason that had
nothing to do with the art: the bloom was on and this was not reaching it.
and the pipeline sharpens them: a 32-square glow goes through a threefold upscale and a
detail pass on the way here, which is right for a plank and wrong for light, because
the one thing light has no business having is an edge. The blur is applied to the
brightness and the alpha together, so the shape stays the shape and only its border
softens.
Feathered at the border, by nineteen per cent of each axis, and this is the fix a blur
was the wrong tool for. What made a lit window read as a card was never the picture -
it was the quad's own edge, which no amount of softening inside the sheet can reach.
The alpha is taken to nothing before it arrives at any border, so the quad has no edge
left to show. Per axis rather than by radius, because these sheets are not squares:
light_02 is a six-by-192 strip, and a radius measured off the long side blurred the
short one out of existence.
And blurred as well, which is the part a feather alone does not do. Feathering dissolves
the quad's border; what is left inside it is still MU's painted shape, and on a window
that reads as a lit picture rather than as light coming through an opening. The blur is
measured against the *short* axis of the sheet - light_02 is six pixels by 192 - because
a radius taken off the long side wipes the short one out entirely, which is the mistake
that turned a window into a flat yellow band the first time.
Nineteen per cent and not the thirty-four it was briefly set to. A feather eats its
fraction from *both* ends of an axis, so thirty-four takes sixty-eight per cent of the
whole - and light_02's short axis is six pixels. The lit window went completely
transparent: the pane disappeared out of its own opening, which is the fault the feather
exists to prevent, arriving from the other side.
Raised again, from 1.6 to 3.2, and the reason is that the town moved under it. 1.6 was
chosen against the old daylight rig; the darker rig then had its exposure lifted twice and
the sun raised, and the same pane that read clearly at 1.6 went invisible inside a wall
that had got brighter while the feather and the blur made the glow itself fainter. A glow
is only ever bright *relative* to what it hangs in, so this number has to move whenever
that does.
